title: The oldest papyrus texts in Egypt are a work crew's logbook.
description:
The oldest papyrus texts in Egypt are a work crew's logbook. Pierre Tallet's team found them at Wadi al-Jarf, on the Red Sea coast, in 2013.

It was written around 2560 BC, near the end of Khufu's reign. Wikipedia dates the papyri to about 2560 to 2550 BC.

Merer, an inspector, shipped limestone by boat from Tura to Giza. Tallet believes the blocks were for the outer casing, though the log never says where the stones went.

Merer reported to Ankhhaf, a nobleman and half brother of Khufu. Ankhhaf was overseer of Ra-shi-Khufu, the harbour at Giza.

The crew ate meat, poultry, fish and beer. Smithsonian Magazine reports that they were well provisioned. Mark Lehner's digs at Giza uncovered apartment blocks that might have housed as many as 20,000 people.

The oldest paperwork in Egypt is about moving stone and feeding the crew.

Sources:
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diary_of_Merer: read. Established that the papyri were found and excavated in 2013 by a French mission under Pierre Tallet and Gregory Marouard; that they are the oldest known papyri with text; that Merer held the title of inspector; that the log records white limestone blocks shipped by boat from the Tura quarries to Giza; that the text does not say where the stones were to be used, with Tallet believing the outer casing; and that Ankhhaf, half brother of Khufu, is called a nobleman and overseer of Ra-shi-Khufu.
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wadi_al-Jarf: read. Established the site on the Red Sea coast, that excavation resumed in 2011 under Tallet and Marouard, that the discovery was announced in April 2013, that the papyri are the oldest ever found in Egypt, and that they date to about 2560 to 2550 BC, the end of Khufu's reign.
- https://www.smithsonianmag.com/history/ancient-egypt-shipping-mining-farming-economy-pyramids-180956619/: read. Established that Tallet found the papyri in 2013, that Merer shipped limestone from Tura to Giza, that the noble Ankhhaf was Khufu's half brother, that the workers were provisioned with meat, poultry, fish and beer, and that Mark Lehner's excavations uncovered apartment blocks at Giza that might have housed as many as 20,000 people.
